column3: Has a specific luxury scent in mind and is testing whether the copy holds; naming the original is the entire search intent.
Wants the cheap bottle held against the expensive one; the physical comparison is the proof of equivalence.
Cannot afford the house but knows the house; putting the original in frame is both the claim and the flattery.
Owns a wall of bottles and is trusted precisely because he has smelled everything; the shelf behind him is the credential.
Buys four for the price of three and stays for the scarf; the free object is what tips the basket.
Interested in a single ingredient expressed several ways; one ingredient, four moods turns a range into a tasting flight.
Wants to see it worn on skin at close range rather than photographed as an object.
Reads a pear and a vanilla pod as the fragrance note list; the styling is the description.
Buys what will look right on rumpled linen; the intimacy of the setting is the selling.
Wants the whole collection in one frame so she can pick a favourite from a family.
Shops within a retailer's certification badge; the seal is the shortlist she buys from.
Reached at the point of a store haul; a full Sephora bag reads as a shopping trip rather than an ad.

Wants a scent that belongs to a t-shirt and shorts rather than an evening; the setting sets the occasion.
Chooses by flavour vocabulary; deep, boozy and addictive is a taste description, not a smell one.
Unwilling to commit blind to a full bottle; a coffret is permission to be indecisive.
Attracted by the archive presentation; the row of samples suggests a library rather than a shop.
Wants the botanicals laid out beside the bottle; the deconstruction is the authenticity claim.
Buying a considered gift for someone whose taste she does not know; a sample set removes the risk of guessing wrong.
Buying the workshop and the hands; the maker in frame is what justifies the price.
Buys a scent that says exactly what it is on the label; italian citrus needs no further explanation.
Wants fragrance without the pretension; a bottle that admits it does not know what it is flatters her scepticism.
Buys the object as much as the scent; an iridescent steamed-glass bottle is the reason to post it.
Wants the concept narrated by whoever thought of it; the animated explanation is the content.
Scenting a house rather than a body; the diffuser placed in a styled room is the aspiration.
Judges the device on whether it suits the shelf; it must read as decor before it reads as appliance.
Buys into the arrival; the box being carried in is the emotional payoff being sold.

Wants her home to smell washed rather than perfumed; crisp laundry is the exact target.
Reads restraint as seriousness; cherished by many is as close to a boast as she wants to hear.
Buys the amber bottles as a set for how they will look in a bathroom others will see.
Spends disproportionately on an ordinary moment; framing hand care beside a loo roll is the joke and the point.
